A minor release that closes three reported issues, finishes the remaining half of two more that
the tracker closed alongside 2.0.1, and changes how the plugin decides where a slice begins. One
new message id is on by default, several existing checks reach shapes they did not reach before,
and one long standing definition has moved from the shape of a path to the contents of the
filesystem.

Unlike 2.0.1, this release can raise your report count as well as lower it. Read "What moves"
below before comparing numbers across the upgrade. Nothing here requires a configuration
change: no option was renamed, no default was flipped for an existing check, and the new
option added by this release only turns a new check off.

## New checks

### `export ... from` is a dependency (#27)

`layers-slices` visited import declarations only, so a re-export bypassed the layer and slice
checks that the equivalent import went through. Re-exports are now visited, and a re-export is
judged exactly as the import of the same path would be.

An upward re-export, in `src/entities/user/model/reexports-features-upward.ts`:

```ts
export { loginUser } from 'src/features/auth';
```

> You cannot import layer "features" into "entities" (shared -> entities -> features -> widgets -> pages -> processes -> app)

A re-export between two slices of one layer is reported the same way, and so is
`export * from`. Type-only re-exports are exempt under `allowTypeImports`, which is on by
default, in all three spellings: `export type { X } from`, `export type * from`, and the
inline `export { type X } from`.

How much this adds depends entirely on what your barrel files re-export. On the eight public
FSD projects this release was measured against it added exactly one report, from one statement:
`workout-cool`'s `src/features/workout-builder/index.ts` forwards a sibling slice on its third
line. That is a fact about those eight barrels and not a promise about yours. The shapes that
stay silent are listed under the next heading, and a barrel built only out of them adds
nothing.

### The pass-through re-export (`pass-through-reexport`)

Once re-exports are dependencies, a second shape becomes visible: a file that re-exports a
**lower** layer, forwarding it through its own layer to whoever imports the file. Importing
downward is legal, so this is not a layer violation, but the re-export makes the higher layer
a proxy for the lower one and hides the real dependency from every consumer.

It has its own message id, `pass-through-reexport`, and it is **on by default**. At default
options it did not fire once on the eight projects this release was measured against. Again,
that is a fact about those barrels: a type-only re-export is exempt by default, and where a
barrel forwards a lower layer as a value the check fires. How loud it is in your project
depends entirely on whether your barrels do that, so it is worth a look before you upgrade a
large codebase.

In `src/widgets/nav/index.ts`:

```ts
export { createUser } from 'src/entities/user';
```

> Re-export from layer "entities" forwards it through "widgets", import it directly instead

The fix is for the consumer to import `src/entities/user` directly. If you use pass-through
barrels deliberately, turn the check off with the new `allowPassThroughReexports` option:

```js
import featureSliced from '@conarti/eslint-plugin-feature-sliced';

export default [
  featureSliced({
    layersSlices: {
      allowPassThroughReexports: true,
    },
  }),
];
```

The option defaults to `false` and affects nothing else: it silences the
`pass-through-reexport` message id and leaves every other check of `layers-slices` alone.

What does **not** report, so you can predict the blast radius:

* a re-export that stays inside one slice, which is what a slice public api is made of;
* a re-export between two files of a layer that has no slices, such as `shared` or `app`;
* a type-only re-export in any of its three spellings;
* a re-export of a layer above this one, which is reported as `can-not-import` instead.

The check does not care whether the file is an `index` file. A plain module inside a segment
that re-exports from a lower layer is reported as well, for instance
`src/features/profile/model/reexports-shared-value.ts` re-exporting `src/shared/lib/format-date`.

### A default import combined with inline type specifiers (#38)

`import config, { type FooType } from 'src/app/config'` was silent. The declaration was
treated as type-only because every **named** specifier was a type, and the default specifier
was never consulted. The default specifier is a value import, so it is now reported:

```ts
import config, { type FooType } from 'src/app/config';
```

> You cannot import layer "app" into "entities" (...)

Where the same declaration also carries a value named specifier, both are reported now where
only the named one was before. See "What moves".

## Changed behaviour

### The slice boundary is read from the filesystem

This is the deepest change in the release, and it has no configuration.

Until now a slice was derived from the shape of the path: the folder before the first
recognized segment name, or the last folder when the path held no segment. A path alone cannot
tell a folder inside a slice from a slice of its own, nor a group folder from either, and 2.0.1
could only narrow that by hand, one shape at a time.

The plugin now asks the disk. Between the layer and the first configured segment it walks the
folders of the path and settles on the **deepest** one that holds a public api file. Deepest
rather than shallowest, because two folders that each hold a public api file sit in different
branches and can never collapse onto one another.

A public api file is an `index` file and nothing else: `index.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`,
`.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.mts`, `.cts`, `.vue` or `.svelte`. A colocated `index.d.ts`,
`index.test.ts`, `index.module.css` or `index.html` does not turn its folder into a slice.

Two consequences worth stating plainly:

* A folder name carrying punctuation no longer hides its slice. With an `index.ts` on
  `entities/(shop)/ShopA`, an import that reaches past that public api, such as
  `entities/(shop)/ShopA/ui/Button`, was silent on 2.0.1 and is reported here, as long as the
  file doing the importing lies in a slice the plugin can resolve as well. That condition is
  easy to leave out when you build the example. An importer at `src/pages/home/index.ts`
  reports, and so does one at `src/pages/home/ui/Page.ts` when `pages/home` holds an `index.ts`
  of its own. The same importer at `src/pages/home/ui/Page.ts` with no `index.ts` on
  `pages/home`, and one at `src/pages/home/A.ts` in a `home` folder that holds no `index` file
  at all, are both silent: the importing side is unresolved, so the joint fallback described
  under "When the probe cannot answer" below applies and takes the imported side down with it.
  The same was measured for a folder spelled `[shop]`, `shop.group` or `shop+group` in that
  position, and for a slice spelled `(user)` or `user+x` sitting directly on its layer. Plainly
  spelled names in the same positions, `shop-group`, `_shop` and `user`, reported on both
  versions and from every one of those importers, so this turns on the spelling and not on
  grouping. Where no folder in range holds a public api file, on either side of the import, the
  old answer stands and the import stays silent.
* A folder inside a slice is no longer a slice. `entities/user/hooks` alongside
  `entities/user/components`, with the `index.ts` on `user`, is one slice, and imports between
  the two folders stop being cross-slice imports.

**When the probe cannot answer**, the path heuristic decides, exactly as before. That happens
when the path cannot be made relative to the project root, or when no folder in range holds a
public api file. The two definitions are never mixed: if either side of a comparison is
unresolved, both sides fall back together. This is close to 2.0.1 behaviour and is intended to
be, but it is not asserted to be identical to it, because that identity has not been proven.

**Caching and editors.** The answer is memoised per directory for the lifetime of the process.
For a command line run that is the run. In a long lived editor or language server process it
is the lifetime of that process, so a public api file you add or delete is not noticed until
the process restarts. If a report looks wrong right after you create or remove an `index.ts`,
restart the ESLint server before filing a bug.

**Cost.** Reading directories puts I/O on the lint path, which is why the cache exists. It was
timed rather than guessed at, over repeated runs of the same projects, and no cost was
detectable: every difference measured was smaller than the spread between repetitions of the
same run, and the release came out faster than the previous version as often as slower. No
percentage is quoted here on purpose, because any single figure drawn from those runs would be
reporting noise as though it were a result.

### Folders that merge into their slice

Because a folder inside a slice is no longer a slice of its own, several path-derived slice
names now resolve to one folder. Imports between them stop being cross-slice imports and their
reports disappear. On the eight public FSD projects this release was measured against, this is
where 14 of the 16 disappearing reports come from, and 13 of the 14 are the same picture: a
slice folder holding an `index.ts`, sub-folders beside it holding none, and a file in one
sub-folder importing another. The sub-folder holding the importing file was one of `__tests__`,
`actions`, `hooks`, `libs/hooks`, `gallery` and `list`; on the imported side the folders were
`actions`, `album`, `hooks`, `libs/constants`, `schema` and `track`. The fourteenth differs
only in its target: the importing file sits in a sub-folder as the others do, but what it
imports is a file lying directly in the slice folder rather than in a second sub-folder.

The shape to look for in your own project is that one: a folder with an `index.ts` whose
sub-folders have none, with something importing across those sub-folders. An `@x`
cross-import folder that holds no `index` file of its own merges the same way, into the slice
that holds it.

A merge is not the same thing as a lost report. Across those eight projects the resolver merges
23 groups of folders in all, and most of them cost nothing you can see: 5 of the 23 move a
report and the other 18 move none, because nothing imports across the merged names. The 23 are
enumerated project by project in `2.1.0-merged-folders.md`, beside this file.

A merge can also produce a report rather than remove one. Where an import that now stays inside
one slice was written absolutely, `absolute-relative` asks for it to be relative instead, and
that accounts for 10 of the 13 new reports on those eight projects.

The failure mode this design exists to avoid is two sibling slices that each carry a public api
merging into one, which would silence a genuine cross-slice report. It did not occur in any of
the 14: in every one of them, only the outer folder held a public api file.

### A checkout under a directory named after a layer

Every search for a layer name starts below the project root rather than at the start of the
absolute path, so an ancestor directory that happens to carry a layer name is not mistaken for
the layer. A project living in a folder called `shared`, `entities`, `pages` or any other
configured layer name answers exactly as the same project under a neutral directory.

Nothing changes for you here. 2.0.1 already answered the same way under any of those parent
names, and this is recorded because the filesystem resolution introduced above had to be built
so as to keep it that way.

### `absolute-relative` reads the `segments` setting (#37)

The rule resolved the slice of a path against a built-in segment list and ignored the
configured one, so an absolute import that stayed inside a single slice was not reported when
that slice used a custom segment name. It now receives the configured list. Combined with the
filesystem resolution above, the shape in the issue is reported from both directions.

### `no-cross-segment-reexport` reads the `segments` setting

The other half of #35. The rule matched sibling folder names against the built-in segment list
and ignored the configured one. It now receives the configured list, and a configured segment
name is where the slice ends.

The example in the issue is not a new report. `entities/cart/services/index.ts` re-exporting
`../model`, with `segments: ['services']` configured, is reported at the same position with the
same message on 2.0.1 and here. What the setting changes is where the slice ends: declare
`services` a segment and the slice stays at `cart`, so the two folders stand in segment
position; leave it undeclared and `services/index.ts` is read as a slice public api of its own,
and the same file is silent here.

Three movements were measured at default options, on folders whose names are not built-in
segment names:

* A re-export between two such sibling folders that hold no `index` file of their own was
  silent on 2.0.1 and is reported here. This follows from the filesystem slice resolution
  rather than from the `segments` list: declaring the same two names as segments produces the
  same report.
* Where the re-exporting folder holds its own `index` file and the folder it reads from does
  not, the re-exporting folder is a slice, so the re-export no longer crosses anything. It was
  reported on 2.0.1 and is silent here.
* Where both folders hold their own `index` file they are two slices, so the re-export is not a
  cross-segment one at all. It is reported by `layers-slices` as `can-not-import` instead, so
  the rule id on that line changes.

### Layers written into `settings` by hand are normalized where they are read

`featureSliced()` writes the layer list into `settings['@conarti/feature-sliced'].layers` in the
normalized `{ name, hasSlices }` form, and the factory stays the documented way to configure the
plugin. Some projects write that setting by hand instead, and four shapes of hand written list
behaved badly. Each was measured on both built bundles, over one project that exercises the
cross layer check and both public api checks at once.

* A list of plain names, `['shared', 'entities', ...]`, answered exactly as an empty list did.
  The cross layer check stopped reporting and a public api message took its place on the same
  line. The failure was silent and partial, which is the worst shape it could have.
* A list of objects carrying `name` but no `hasSlices` gave a third answer again: the cross
  layer report stayed, and public api reports the factory does not produce appeared beside it.
* A list holding an entry whose `name` is `null` degraded quietly, dropping the cross layer
  report and saying nothing.
* A list holding an entry that is not an object at all, a bare `null` or a number, threw a
  `TypeError` out of the rule and ended the lint of that file, putting a stack trace where a
  report belongs.

All four now answer exactly as the same layers answer through the factory. One entry that can
name no layer sends the whole list back to the default layers rather than dropping only that
entry, and a missing or `null` `layers` key still gives the defaults. The factory route is
unchanged and still refuses a malformed list: `featureSliced({ layers: [null] })` throws on
both versions.

One further change here is not a fix, and it can silence a report. An empty hand written list,
`layers: []`, is now honoured as a project with no layers, so the check that flags an `index`
file sitting directly on a layer stops firing under it. On 2.0.1 that check still fired. If you
set `layers: []` by hand, expect `layers-public-api-not-allowed` to go quiet.

### The layer public api check sees custom layers and dot paths (#34)

The check that flags an `index` file sitting directly on a layer looked only for the built-in
layer names and did not fire under a directory whose name begins with a dot. Both are fixed:
an `index.ts` on a custom layer such as `domain` is reported, and a checkout under `.cache/`,
`.worktrees/` or any other dotted directory is checked like any other.

## What moves

Read this section before comparing report counts or pinning positions across the upgrade.

**Re-exports go from silent to reported.** `layers-slices` visited no re-export at all on
2.0.1, so every shape named above was silent as far as that rule was concerned. That is not the
same as the file being silent: the single statement that became a new `layers-slices` report on
the eight measured projects already carried a `public-api` report on 2.0.1, at the same line
and the same column. How much this adds is a question about your barrel files and not about
this release: across the eight measured projects 13 reports appeared, and exactly one of them
came from a re-export. Ten were `absolute-relative` `must-be-relative-path` and two were
`public-api` `should-be-from-public-api`, all of them consequences of the slice boundary moving
rather than of re-exports becoming visible.

**Where a re-export report lands.** When every named specifier is a value, the report sits on
the source string. When the declaration mixes value and inline type specifiers, it sits on
each offending value specifier instead, which is where the equivalent import has always put
it. `export { type FooType, foo } from '...'` is reported on `foo`, not on the path.

**A declaration that mixes value and inline type specifiers yields one report per value
specifier.** `export { a, type A, b } from '...'` produces two reports, on `a` and on `b`.
Without an inline type in the declaration there is one report on the source string, so
`export { a, b } from '...'` produces one. This matches the import side exactly, which has
always behaved this way.

**One import shape goes from one report to two.** From #38 above:
`import config, { type FooType, foo } from '...'` produced a single report on `foo` and now
produces two, the additional one on the default specifier `config`. They arrive in source
order, so `config` at column 8 is the first of the two and `foo` the second. It is the only
shape measured in which a report that already existed becomes more than one.

**Some reports disappear.** Across the eight measured projects, at default options, 16 reports
disappeared, in two shapes, because the slice boundary can move either way. A hand written
`layers: []` can silence one more, which is described under "Layers written into `settings` by
hand" above and did not arise on any of the eight.

*The boundary moves shallower.* A folder inside a slice stops being a slice of its own, so an
import between two such folders stops being a cross-slice import. These are the merged folders
described above, and they account for 14 of the 16.

*The boundary moves deeper.* A folder that carries its own `index` file becomes a slice where
the path heuristic did not make it one. Two shapes were measured:

* A folder whose name merely *begins* with a built-in segment name, such as `ui-kit-button` or
  `model-store`. 2.0.1 matched the segment name by prefix, cut the folder name short and
  reported an import of that folder as a deep import, naming a public api path that does not
  exist: `src/features/probe-kit-button` for `src/features/probe/ui-kit-button`. It is silent
  now, and that was rechecked for each of the six built-in segment names, against a control
  name that shares no prefix with any of them and is silent on both versions. This one was a
  false positive, and it is the remaining 2 of the 16. Both are in `moonlogs`, where 2.0.1
  named `@/features-token/api-token-create` and `@/features-token/api-token-edit` for imports
  of `@/features/api-token/api-token-create` and `@/features/api-token/api-token-edit`.
* A re-export out of a folder that holds its own `index` file into a sibling folder of its
  former slice, which was a `no-cross-segment-reexport` and is not one once the re-exporting
  folder is a slice.

## Known limitations

**A relative specifier that climbs above the ESLint working directory.** If you point ESLint
at a directory below your project root, typically the FSD root such as `src`, a relative
import that leaves that directory, such as a file in `src` importing the project's own
`package.json`, lies under no root the plugin can anchor on and is searched as written. When
the checkout also sits under a directory carrying a configured layer name, that search finds
the layer in the parent directory and reports a violation that is not there. It is reported by
`absolute-relative` as `must-be-absolute-path`, and in this release by `layers-slices` as well.

Both conditions are needed. Under a neutrally named parent directory nothing is reported, and
with the working directory at the project root nothing is reported under any parent name. The
`absolute-relative` half of this predates 2.1.0; the `layers-slices` half is new here.

Pointing ESLint's working directory at the project root rather than at the FSD root avoids it
entirely, and is the recommended workaround.

## Issue status

`#27`, `#37` and `#38` were open against this release and are closed by it.

`#34` and `#35` were already closed on the tracker, in the same batch as 2.0.1. Each of them
had two halves, and 2.0.1 fixed one half of each: the dot-path matching of `ignoreFiles` and
`ignoreImports` for `#34`, and the file name read as a segment for `#35`. The other half of
each is what this release fixes, under the same issue number. Neither has anything outstanding
after this.

`#41` is closed on the tracker too, and this release widens the ground it is closed on. Wherever
the filesystem can resolve the slice, the ambiguity the issue described is gone. Where no folder
in range holds a public api file, the slice is still derived from the path and that ambiguity
stands.
